items.name: Hold
items.definition: Any shaped grip bolted to the wall for hands or feet.
items.kid: The bumps on the wall you grab or stand on.
items.demo: Touch three holds and name their colors.
items.explanation: A climbing hold is a shaped grip, usually bolted to a wall, that you grab or stand on. Holds are arranged in paths called routes by route setters, and they come in many shapes (jugs, crimps, pinches, slopers, volumes).
items.whyItMatters: Naming hold types helps kids choose feet and hands on purpose, and it is the language of route reading.
items.howToCoachIt: Touch and name a jug, a crimp, a pinch, a sloper, and a foothold on the wall in front of you. Momentum's Mo Mini list starts with those basic names.

items.name: Jug
items.definition: A large, deep, positive hold that is easy to grip.
items.kid: A big hold shaped like a jug handle.
items.demo: Hang from a jug and from a small hold; compare.
items.explanation: A jug (also called a bucket in the glossary) is a large handhold that is very easy to use. The photo attached here is a large, positive indoor speed-climbing hold — an honest stand-in for that ‘easy to hold’ shape, not a training cue to climb speed routes.
items.whyItMatters: Jugs are the right place to teach new movement, rests, and straight arms, because the hands can hold on while the feet and hips learn the skill.
items.howToCoachIt: Ask the group to find three jugs and then do a drill (hover feet, robot arms, or a mantle press) only on those large holds first.

images.alt: A large, positive indoor speed-climbing hold with a deep, easy-to-grab shape. It is shown here as a close-up of a jug-like hold, not as a cue to practise speed climbing.

items.name: Crimp
items.definition: A small, thin edge held with the fingertips; also the grip used on it.
items.kid: A tiny ledge you hold with your fingertips.
items.demo: Show open-hand and half-crimp on a big edge; no full crimp for young kids.
items.explanation: A crimp, or crimper, is a small, thin edge held with the fingertips; the word also names the grip used on it. An open-hand or half-crimp position uses the fingertips without closing the thumb over the index finger. A full crimp, with the thumb closed, loads the fingers more aggressively. The BMC notes that forces from the crimping action are especially implicated in finger growth-plate stress fractures in teenage climbers. The Science of Climbing Training adds that crimping puts most stress on the A2 and A4 finger pulleys, and reports research linking pulley tears to crimping without a thorough warm-up (at least 100 moves of easier climbing).
items.whyItMatters: Thin edges show up often, but full crimping is a poor default for youth fingers that are still growing. Open-hand and half-crimp on larger edges are the grips this program demonstrates first.
items.howToCoachIt: Show open-hand and half-crimp on a big edge. Do not teach a full, thumb-closed crimp to young climbers. If a climber has persistent finger pain, stop loading that finger and get it checked — do not work through it. See growth-plate. Only move to small edges after plenty of easy climbing on big holds.

images.alt: Close-up insets of fingertip grips on small edges, including more open and more closed (full-crimp) positions. Use this to name the positions; do not use it as a cue for youth climbers to train a full, thumb-closed crimp.

items.name: Sloper
items.definition: A rounded hold with no edge; it relies on friction and body position.
items.kid: A round, smooth hold you hug with your whole hand.
items.demo: Hold it with straight arms and hips low and pulled in high.
items.explanation: A sloper is a hold whose surface slopes down toward the ground, with very little positive lip. It is held with open-handed friction and body position — often a straight arm and hips or shoulders placed so the hand is pressing in and down — rather than with a crimp.
items.whyItMatters: Slopers punish a pull that is not lined up with the hold. They are a good classroom for body position and straight arms, once the climber has some basic tension.
items.howToCoachIt: Start with a large sloper on moderate ground. Cue a full-hand contact, a straight arm, and hips or feet placed so the body weight loads the hold instead of peeling off it.

images.alt: A climber’s open hand pressed onto a rounded, sloping hold with little or no positive edge.

items.name: Pinch
items.definition: A hold squeezed between thumb and fingers.
items.kid: A hold you pinch like a crab claw.
items.demo: Squeeze a pinch with and without the thumb.

items.name: Pocket
items.definition: A hole in a hold for one or more fingers (one-finger pockets, monos, are not for youth).
items.kid: A hole you poke fingers into.
items.demo: Count how many fingers fit.

items.name: Sidepull
items.definition: A hold facing sideways, pulled toward the body's midline.
items.kid: A hold you pull sideways, like opening a sliding door.
items.demo: Lean away from a sidepull to make it work.

items.name: Undercling
items.definition: A hold facing down, gripped palm-up with feet high.
items.kid: A hold you grab from underneath, like lifting a box.
items.demo: Grip palm-up and walk feet higher.

items.name: Gaston
items.definition: A hold pushed outward with the elbow out, thumb down.
items.kid: A hold you push open, like opening elevator doors.
items.demo: Mime opening elevator doors, then on the wall.

items.name: Volume
items.definition: A large hollow feature bolted to the wall, often with holds on it.
items.kid: A giant shape on the wall you can stand or grab on.
items.demo: Climb onto a volume and stand on it.
items.explanation: A volume is a large, hollow, bolted-on feature on an indoor wall. It may itself have smaller holds on it, and climbers can stand, smear, or press on its faces and edges.
items.whyItMatters: Volumes change the shape of the wall: they create new angles, rests, smears, and mantles that are not obvious from a hold list alone.
items.howToCoachIt: Have climbers climb onto a low volume and stand on it, then find a hold on it and a smear on its side. Volume Stay and mantle practice both use a large volume as the classroom.

images.alt: Indoor lead wall with several large, angular volumes bolted to the panels, plus a climber clipping a quickdraw. The volumes are the teaching point here; the clipping context is Ages 12+ and 14+.

items.name: Foothold
items.definition: A hold used for feet; small ones are called chips or jibs.
items.kid: A hold for your feet.
items.demo: Find the smallest foothold in reach.
items.explanation: A foothold is any place you stand: a bolt-on hold, a chip, a volume, or a smear on the wall itself. Wikipedia's glossary treats a hold as a place to cling, grip, jam, press, or stand.
items.whyItMatters: Looking at the foothold before you place the foot is the shared idea behind quiet feet, sticky feet, hover feet, and downclimbing.
items.howToCoachIt: Ask the climber to point to the next foothold, then watch whether the foot lands there quietly and stays.

items.name: Hold Direction
items.definition: Which way a hold's best surface faces; it decides how to pull. Positive holds are incut; negative ones slope away.
items.kid: Which way the hold's grab side points.
items.demo: Find the 'smile' of a hold before grabbing.

items.name: Smear
items.definition: Pressing the sole flat on the wall with no foothold, using friction.
items.kid: Pressing your shoe flat on the wall to stick.
items.demo: Walk feet up blank wall while holding a jug.
items.explanation: Smearing is using friction from the sole of the climbing shoe when there are no good footholds to stand on. It is a central skill of slab climbing, which emphasizes balance, footwork, and smearing on walls that are less than vertical.
items.whyItMatters: If kids only hunt for edges, they miss a lot of useful feet, especially on slab.
items.howToCoachIt: Start on a low-angle slab. Weight the whole sole and keep the hip over the foot. Contrast it with edging on a nearby narrow foothold.

images.alt: Close view of a climbing shoe smearing on rock, the sole pressed flat to use friction.
Climber standing on a friction slab with weight over smeared feet.

sources.title: Glossary: smearing, edging, slab, slab climbing

items.name: Edging
items.definition: Standing on a hold with the inside or outside edge of the shoe.
items.kid: Standing on the side of your shoe.
items.demo: Inside edge, then outside edge, on the same hold.
items.explanation: Edging uses the edge of the climbing shoe on a narrow foothold. When there is no foothold to edge on, smearing (friction from the sole) is used instead.
items.whyItMatters: Choosing an edge or a smear is basic footwork. Precise placement still matters for both.
items.howToCoachIt: Find a small edge and a blank patch of wall side by side. Have the climber edge one foot and smear the other, looking at each placement first. No accurate close-up edging photo was available for this draft, so demo on the wall.

items.name: Toeing In
items.definition: Pulling with the toes to keep feet on steep terrain.
items.kid: Pulling the hold toward you with your toes.
items.demo: See Drag a Hold.

items.name: Heel Hook
items.definition: Placing the heel on a hold and pulling with the hamstring.
items.kid: Hooking your heel on a hold like a hand.
items.demo: Heel hook a big hold at waist height.
items.explanation: A heel hook uses the back of the heel to apply pressure on a hold for balance or leverage. It is different from a toe hook, which presses the top of the toes under a hold to pull the body in.
items.whyItMatters: A good heel hook can take weight off the hands and help the hips stay close, especially on steep terrain or a traverse.
items.howToCoachIt: Start with a large, obvious heel on a volume or rail at a comfortable height. Set the heel, then move the hips, then move a hand. Keep pads closed underneath.

images.alt: Indoor heel hook with the back of the heel set on a hold, body and free leg visible.

items.name: Toe Hook
items.definition: Hooking the top of the toes behind a hold.
items.kid: Hooking the top of your toes on a hold.
items.demo: Toe hook a volume edge.
items.explanation: A toe hook is pressing the upper side of the toes under or behind a hold to pull the body in, most often on overhangs and volumes. It is the opposite idea of a heel hook, which uses the heel. The main muscle doing the pulling is the tibialis anterior, at the front of the shin.
items.whyItMatters: On steep ground a toe hook can keep the hips in and stop the feet from cutting, if the hook is placed with intention and the shoe stays on.
items.howToCoachIt: Start on a large volume edge or a big hold on an easy overhang. Show the top of the shoe making contact, then a gentle pull-in, and a calm release. Keep the first tries low.

images.alt: Climber hooking the top of the toes around a hold on steep terrain, pulling the body in toward the wall.

sources.title: The Science of Climbing Training
sources.author: Sergio Consuegra

items.name: Foot Swap
items.definition: Replacing one foot with the other on the same hold.
items.kid: Swapping feet on one hold.
items.demo: See Foot Switching.
items.explanation: A foot swap (also a foot switch) is replacing one foot with the other on the same hold, so the feet can be reorganized for the next move without losing the hold.
items.whyItMatters: Without a calm swap, climbers hop, match badly, or end up with the wrong foot forward for the next reach. It is a basic organizing skill on vertical and slab.
items.howToCoachIt: On a large foothold, practise a slow swap: weight on the hands and the other foot, place the new foot, then take the old one off. Cue quiet contacts rather than a jump-switch.

items.name: Frontstep
items.definition: Standing on the inside edge, hips square to the wall.
items.kid: Standing facing the wall on your big toe side.
items.demo: See Quick Step.

items.name: Backstep
items.definition: Standing on the outside edge with the hip turned in.
items.kid: Standing on your pinky-toe side, hip turned to the wall.
items.demo: See Quick Step.
items.explanation: A backstep uses the outside edge of the shoe (the little-toe side) on a foothold, with the hip turned in toward the wall. It is a different hip and foot orientation from a standard inside-edge step, and it often sets up a drop knee or a longer reach on the same-side hand.
items.whyItMatters: Turning the hip in can bring the body closer to the wall and make a reach possible without pulling harder. Same-hand, same-foot still usually applies; a back flag is a named exception.
items.howToCoachIt: On a vertical wall with an obvious foothold out to the side, ask the climber to stand on the outside edge and turn the hip in, then compare it with an inside-edge stance on the same hold.

images.alt: Climber with the hip turned in, standing on the outside edge of the shoe — a backstep.

items.name: High Step
items.definition: Placing a foot high, near the hip or hand.
items.kid: A big step way up high.
items.demo: High step and stand up.
items.explanation: A high step is placing a foot on a hold that is significantly higher than usual, often near the hips or hands, then weighting it to stand up. Momentum groups high steps with toe placement and body position: sometimes the body is stretched, sometimes scrunched, and both can be useful.
items.whyItMatters: Kids often avoid a high foot and over-reach with the hands. A committed high step can make the next hand easy.
items.howToCoachIt: On a vertical wall with large holds, ask for a high foot, eyes on the hold, then a stand-up with hips over that foot. High/Low Feet (10–20 min in Momentum's contact drills) contrasts scrunched feet with a stretched, tip-toe position.

images.alt: Climber making a high step on a boulder, one foot raised high while the body stays close to the wall.

items.name: Rock Over
items.definition: Shifting weight over a high foot to stand on it.
items.kid: Moving your body over a high foot and standing up.
items.demo: See Skipping Holds.

items.name: Quiet Feet
items.definition: Placing feet without noise, which signals precision.
items.kid: Putting your feet down so quietly nobody hears.
items.demo: See Silent Feet.
items.explanation: Quiet feet means placing each foot without noise, which is a signal of a precise, controlled placement. Gresham treats precise footwork as a generic drill: not which kind of placement (edge or smear), but how quietly and carefully the foot is set.
items.whyItMatters: Noisy, slapping feet usually mean the climber did not look and is not standing on the foot with confidence.
items.howToCoachIt: Momentum's Quiet Sticky Ninja Feet drill (5–10 min): look at the hold first, place a silent, firm foot, and stand up on it. Do this on easy traverses or routes. Do not turn missed silence into an elimination game.

sources.title: Neil Gresham: Improve Your Movement — precise footwork

items.name: Drop Knee
items.definition: Turning one knee down and in to bring the hip to the wall.
items.kid: Twisting your knee down so your hip touches the wall.
items.demo: Drop knee on two footholds at the same height.
items.explanation: A drop knee (also called an Egyptian) is turning one knee inward and down so the hip comes close to the wall and the reach gets longer. Both feet push through the big toes, and the knee that turns is the one on the same side as the reaching hand. It is a position you pass through — turn in, reach, unwind — and a deep drop knee puts real load on the knee.
items.whyItMatters: On steep ground, a drop knee often buys reach and takes weight off the arms in a way that pulling harder will not. It suits climbers who already have a comfortable backstep, and it should be built gradually.
items.howToCoachIt: Use Drop-Knee Finder: compare the same move hips-square and with the drop knee. Start with close footholds, a shallow turn, and big handholds. Skip very deep or wide drop knees, keep reps low, and stop if the knee twinges. If a climber has tweaked a knee on a drop knee, expect hesitation even after it has healed: the brain keeps guarding a move it links with pain. Rebuild it in small, easy, successful steps (see Rebuild the Move in enrich_v3).

images.alt: Climber with one knee dropped in and down, hip close to the steep wall, reaching with the same-side hand.

items.name: Flagging
items.definition: Placing a leg against the wall without a hold to balance.
items.kid: Sticking a leg out like a tail to keep balance.
items.demo: See Monkey Tails.
items.explanation: Flagging is holding a leg in a position to keep balance, rather than to support weight, often to prevent a barn-door swing. The glossary names three types: a normal flag (free foot stays on the same side), a reverse inside-flag (crosses in front of the standing foot), and a reverse outside-flag (crosses behind). A back-step uses the outside (little-toe) edge of the shoe and often appears with a flag.
items.whyItMatters: When both feet are on the same side of the hands, the body can swing. A flag is the usual fix.
items.howToCoachIt: Build a simple problem where both footholds sit on one side. Let the climber feel the barn-door, then add a flag or a taped box for the free leg. Flag Boxes is the matching drill.

images.alt: Climber in a back-step with the free leg flagged to the side for balance.

items.name: Straight Arms
items.definition: Hanging on extended arms so the skeleton holds weight.
items.kid: Hanging like a monkey with long arms.
items.demo: See Robot Arms.
items.explanation: Straight arms means hanging on extended arms so the skeleton, not bent elbows, holds the weight. Gresham: on steep walls the instinct is to straighten the legs and bend the arms when pumped or scared; the better position is arms as straight as possible, shoulders engaged, hips centred below, legs bent.
items.whyItMatters: Bent-arm hanging tires the pumps quickly. Straight arms are one of Gresham's generic movement drills, alongside precise feet.
items.howToCoachIt: On an easy steep climb, use Robot Arms and Gresham's loop: precise feet, straight arms, relaxed grip. Do not use a hard project for the first look at this cue.

sources.title: Neil Gresham: Improve Your Movement — straight arms, relaxed grip

items.name: Lock-Off
items.definition: Holding a bent arm still while the other hand reaches; strength in a lock-off mostly improves at the exact angle practised.
items.kid: Freezing one arm bent while you reach.
items.demo: See Hover Hands.

sources.title: The Science of Climbing Training
sources.author: Sergio Consuegra

items.name: Dyno
items.definition: A jump where the body leaves contact to catch a hold.
items.kid: A jump to a hold.
items.demo: See Dyno Dash.
items.explanation: A dyno is a dynamic jump or leap to an out-of-reach hold; missing the hold will usually result in a fall. A deadpoint is a more controlled dynamic in which the hold is grabbed at the apex of the movement while other points of contact remain.
items.whyItMatters: Dynos are exciting and easy to overuse. They belong on closed pads or a belay, at a height you have agreed, after the climber can do the same wall statically when the holds allow it.
items.howToCoachIt: Compare a static reach and a short padded dyno to a large hold. Talk about the landing before the first jump. For Ages 12+ and 14+, keep dynamic practice to a few high-quality tries with full rest, and stop when the moves slow down.

images.alt: Indoor climber fully off the wall in mid-air, both feet off, jumping toward the next hold — a clearer dyno than a one-foot dynamic reach.

sources.title: The Science of Climbing Training
sources.author: Sergio Consuegra
sources.chapter: Chapter 8: What Can I Optimise in My Training Sessions?

items.name: Deadpoint
items.definition: A dynamic move catching a hold at the top of the body's movement.
items.kid: A quick reach at the floaty moment.
items.demo: Deadpoint on a big hold.
items.explanation: A deadpoint is a controlled dynamic move: the climber catches the next hold at the exact moment the body stops rising, while the feet (and usually the other hand) stay on the wall. It is not a dyno — if the feet come off, the try was a dyno.
items.whyItMatters: A deadpoint lengthens the reach at a low cost: the body barely leaves the wall, and the climber is not hanging off a slow lock-off. Precision — catching an exact spot on the hold — is the skill being trained.
items.howToCoachIt: On easy boulders, pick 3–4 long reaches and an exact spot on each target. Five tries per move with about a minute of rest. Start on big jugs and a vertical wall; if the feet leave, reset and name the difference.

sources.title: Deadpoint climbing: how to train deadpoints

items.name: Static
items.definition: Slow, controlled movement keeping three points on.
items.kid: Moving slow and smooth like a sloth.
items.demo: See Static and Dynamic.
items.explanation: In this program, static means slow, controlled movement that keeps three points of contact. It is the opposite of a dyno (a jump to an out-of-reach hold). A deadpoint sits in between: a controlled dynamic where the hand arrives at the apex while the other contacts stay on.
items.whyItMatters: Kids often jump when a static move would work. Teaching both words lets them choose the movement the hold actually needs.
items.howToCoachIt: Do the same easy sequence once statically, then ask whether any reach truly needs a jump. Save committed dynos for padded, agreed tries.

items.name: Dynamic
items.definition: Movement using momentum.
items.kid: Moving fast with a swing or jump.
items.demo: See Static and Dynamic.
items.explanation: Dynamic movement uses momentum — a swing, a pop, or a jump — to reach a hold that is hard to get statically. A dyno is the bigger leap, usually leaving the feet; a deadpoint is a smaller, more controlled dynamic that catches the hold at the apex while the feet stay on.
items.whyItMatters: Climbers who only pull statically can get stuck on longer moves. Timing a small dynamic, on a closed pad or a belay, is often less costly than a strained lock-off — but big dynos are easy to overuse and need an agreed height and a clear landing. Holding the target after a fast move also depends on how quickly grip force builds on landing (rate of force development), which the book finds markedly higher in boulderers than in route climbers.
items.howToCoachIt: Compare a static reach and a short, padded dynamic to a large hold. For a jump, talk through the landing first. If the feet stay on and the catch is at the high point, name it a deadpoint, not a dyno.

images.alt: Indoor climber fully off the wall in mid-air, jumping toward the next hold — a clear dynamic / dyno, not a deadpoint (the feet have left the wall).

sources.title: The Science of Climbing Training
sources.author: Sergio Consuegra
sources.chapter: Chapter 7: Analysis of the Main Physiological Factors in Climbing Performance
sources.section: New findings about limiting factors in climbing performance: routes and bouldering

items.name: Match
items.definition: Putting both hands (or feet) on the same hold.
items.kid: Both hands on one hold.
items.demo: Match on a jug.
items.explanation: In this program, a match is putting both hands, or both feet, on the same hold. The glossary also mentions a shadow match, which is a quick hand switch on a hold that only fits one hand; that is a more advanced variant, not the basic class meaning.
items.whyItMatters: Matching is a common way to reorganize for the next reach, and it appears in mantles (hand-foot match) as well as on jugs.
items.howToCoachIt: Start on a jug large enough for two hands. Then try a hand-foot match on a low ledge as part of mantle practice.

items.name: Bump
items.definition: Moving one hand twice in a row to reach a better hold.
items.kid: Moving the same hand again.
items.demo: See Systems Wall Drills.

items.name: Cross Through
items.definition: Reaching one hand over or under the other.
items.kid: Crossing your arms to reach.
items.demo: Cross through on a traverse.

items.name: Mantle
items.definition: Pressing down on a ledge to climb on top of it.
items.kid: Pushing down like getting out of a pool.
items.demo: Mantle a volume.
items.explanation: A mantle (also spelled mantel) is pressing down on a ledge or the top of a volume and bringing the feet up so you can stand on it, like pushing out of a pool. The hands change from pulling to pressing as the chest comes up and over the lip.
items.whyItMatters: Many indoor tops and volumes finish with a press, not another pull. Practising the press on a low volume keeps the skill from becoming a desperate belly flop at the top of a problem.
items.howToCoachIt: Start on a low volume or ledge. Ask for a press, a foot on the lip, and a stand-up, with a clear mat and a step-down if it does not work. See Mantle Practice.

images.alt: Outdoor climber pressing both hands down on a ledge and bringing the body up to stand on top of it — a mantle.

items.name: Layback
items.definition: Pulling on a side edge while pushing feet the opposite way.
items.kid: Pulling and pushing opposite ways on an edge.
items.demo: Layback an arete.
items.explanation: Laybacking (also liebacking) is climbing an edge by side-pulling with both hands and using opposing friction with the feet.
items.whyItMatters: It is a clear example of opposition: hands pull, feet push. It shows up on aretes, crack edges, and some volumes.
items.howToCoachIt: Find a vertical edge or volume rail. Cue pull with the hands, push with the feet, and keep the hips close. Use a height they can downclimb or drop from with pads.

images.alt: Climber laybacking a crack: both hands side-pulling the edge, feet pushing in opposition on the face.

items.name: Stemming
items.definition: Pushing feet and hands against opposing walls.
items.kid: Pushing out on both sides of a corner.
items.demo: Stem in a corner.
items.explanation: Stemming (also called bridging) is climbing opposing walls or a corner by pushing in opposite directions with the feet and hands. Chimneying is the related skill of climbing a cleft large enough for the body.
items.whyItMatters: Opposition can take weight off the arms and even allow a rest. It is also a clear way to feel body tension.
items.howToCoachIt: Use a wide dihedral or two facing volumes. Cue press the feet out. A brief, solid no-hands pause is a useful test on easy stems only.

images.alt: Classic stem / bridge in a wide chimney-like corner, both legs pressing outward.
Climber stemming in an open-book dihedral, feet on opposite walls.

items.name: Knee Bar
items.definition: Wedging the knee and foot between holds to rest.
items.kid: Wedging your knee to rest your arms.
items.demo: Find a knee bar on a volume.

items.name: Cut Feet
items.definition: Feet coming off the wall, usually on steep terrain.
items.kid: When your feet swing off the wall.
items.demo: Show controlled foot return.
items.explanation: Cut feet (also cutting feet, or a cut-loose) is when the feet swing off the wall, usually on steep terrain, leaving the climber hanging from the hands. Sometimes it is planned; often it is a surprise loss of foot pressure.
items.whyItMatters: Unexpected cut feet turn a move into an all-arms moment and can end a try. On a deadpoint drill, feet coming off means the try became a dyno.
items.howToCoachIt: On an easy overhang, have the climber practise a controlled foot return after a small, planned cut. Cue pushing through the feet so they stay on when the goal is a deadpoint or a static reach.

images.alt: Climber on a steep overhang, the kind of terrain where feet can cut loose if pressure through the toes is lost.

sources.title: Deadpoint climbing: how to train deadpoints

items.name: Center of Gravity
items.definition: The body's balance point; climbers keep it over the feet.
items.kid: Your body's balance spot, near your belly button.
items.demo: Stand on one foot and lean.
items.explanation: The centre of gravity is the body's balance point. In this program, climbers learn to keep it over the feet. Gresham's steep-wall position puts the hips centred directly below straight, engaged arms, with the legs bent. A drop-knee is an advanced way to twist the hips — and the centre of gravity — closer to a steep wall.
items.whyItMatters: When the hips drift away from the wall or off the standing foot, feet smear off and arms take the weight.
items.howToCoachIt: On a smear or a hover-feet drill, ask the climber to move the hips over the standing foot. Blok Sessions uses the same cue when a hover starts to swing.

images.alt: Climber on a friction slab with the weight and hips over smeared feet, a clear example of balance over the feet.

sources.title: Neil Gresham: Improve Your Movement — hips centred
Glossary: drop knee (hips and centre of gravity closer to the wall)

items.name: Hips to the Wall
items.definition: Bringing hips close to the wall to shift weight onto feet.
items.kid: Pull your belly or hip toward the wall.
items.demo: Compare hips out and in.

items.name: Three Points of Contact
items.definition: Keeping three limbs on while one moves.
items.kid: Three on, one moves.
items.demo: Count limbs on the wall each move.
items.explanation: Three points of contact means keeping three limbs on the wall while one moves. It is a starting habit for balance on slabs and vertical walls, not a rule that never changes — dynos, flags, and some steep moves deliberately break it.
items.whyItMatters: New climbers often move two limbs at once and get off balance. Counting ‘three on, one moves’ slows the sequence down until foot placements are reliable.
items.howToCoachIt: On an easy slab or vertical wall, have the climber say which limb is moving and count the three that stay on. Later, name the exceptions (a flag, a deadpoint, a planned dyno) so the habit does not block more advanced movement.

items.name: Body Tension
items.definition: Engaging the whole trunk, hips and shoulders, not just the stomach, to keep the feet on and the body controlled.
items.kid: Squeezing your middle so you stay stuck.
items.demo: See Keep the Tension.
items.explanation: Body tension is the core and opposing limbs working together so the feet stay on and the body does not sag or swing. Stemming (pressing in opposite directions) and, on steeper ground, a drop-knee are common ways coaches see that tension.
items.whyItMatters: Without tension, even good handholds are not enough on a steep wall or a wide stem; the feet peel and the arms take all the load.
items.howToCoachIt: Use a wide, large-hold stem and ask the climber to press the feet out. On an overhang, Momentum's drop-knee page notes the climber needs both feet outside the centerline and should be cautious of knee strain; keep repetition limited and warm up the lower body.

items.name: Turning In
items.definition: Rotating the hips so one side faces the wall, adding reach.
items.kid: Twisting your hip to the wall to reach higher.
items.demo: See Pivot Practice.

items.name: Rest Position
items.definition: A low-effort stance on the wall to recover, often with straight arms, resting one hand at a time and breathing slowly.
items.kid: A comfy spot on the wall to rest your arms.
items.demo: See Freeze Traverse.
items.explanation: A rest position is a low-effort stance on the wall used to recover — often with straight arms, weight over the feet or a stem, and resting one hand at a time. A no-hand rest is a fully leg-supported stance that does not require the hands on the wall. This is different from rest, which in this vocabulary means time off the wall.
items.whyItMatters: Climbers who can find a hidden rest climb longer before they pump. A poor ‘rest’ that is still a bent-arm hang does not actually recover the forearms.
items.howToCoachIt: Use Hidden Rest and Top-Rope Rest Hunt: demonstrate a stem, a stance over a big foothold, or hips against a volume, then have climbers find and show one. No-hands rests stay low on a boulder or on top rope. Teach climbers to rest early, before a full pump: on a big hold, let one hand hang loose for about 3–10 seconds, swap, and repeat 4–5 times while breathing slowly. The book reports that shaking out by itself does little.

items.name: Harness
items.definition: Waist belt and leg loops that connect a climber to the rope.
items.kid: The seat you wear to tie into the rope.
items.demo: See Harness Check.
items.explanation: A climbing harness is a sewn, load-bearing waist-and-leg device that the rope and other load-bearing gear attach to. On a standard sit harness the rope is tied through the two tie-in points (bridges). The belay loop is for a belay device or an auto-belay connector, attached with a locking carabiner. Gear loops are for racking only. The usual tie-in knot is the figure-eight follow-through, often backed up by a stopper knot. Always check the knot before climbing.
items.whyItMatters: A waist belt worn too low, a knot through the wrong point, or an unlocked locker is a serious error; the partner check exists to catch it every time.
items.howToCoachIt: Lay the harness out, name waist, legs, belay loop, tie-in points, and gear loops, then put it on and check each other. Petzl: “Tie in to the two tie-in points.” For auto belays, staff permission is required, and TRUBLUE says to clip the belay loop only, not multiple hard points.

items.name: Belay Loop
items.definition: The strong loop on a harness for the belay device.
items.kid: The strongest loop on the front of your harness.
items.demo: Point to it on a harness.
items.explanation: The belay loop is the strong closed loop on the front of a sit harness, and the point to which a belay device or an auto-belay carabiner is attached. It is not the same as the two tie-in points, where the rope is tied through. Gear loops are not load-bearing.
items.whyItMatters: Clipping a device or an auto-belay carabiner to a tie-in point, a gear loop, or both hard points is a serious loading error. Naming the belay loop correctly is the foundation of harness-parts teaching and partner checks.
items.howToCoachIt: In Harness Parts Callout, end by pointing to the belay loop as the only clip-in point for a belay device or auto-belay carabiner (staff permission still required before any auto-belay use) and to the two tie-in points for the rope. Petzl’s harness figures show both clearly.

items.name: Tie-In Points
items.definition: The two harness points the rope goes through to tie in.
items.kid: The two loops your rope goes through.
items.demo: Thread a rope through both.
items.explanation: Tie-in points are the two harness hard points the rope is threaded through when tying in with a figure-8 follow-through — usually one at the waist belt and one at the leg-loop junction, not the belay loop. Petzl’s gym and harness notices show the rope passing through both tie-in points. Clipping in with a carabiner is not a substitute for tying through both tie-in points.
items.whyItMatters: Threading only one point, or tying into the belay loop, changes how a fall loads the harness. This is one of the first things a partner check should trace.
items.howToCoachIt: Use a practice harness on the ground. Have the climber thread both tie-in points, dress the knot, and have a partner trace the rope path before a coach confirms. Petzl’s finished-knot and harness figures are the model.

items.name: Climbing Shoes
items.definition: Snug, sticky rubber shoes for climbing.
items.kid: Special sticky shoes.
items.demo: Feel the rubber.
items.explanation: Climbing shoes are snug footwear with sticky rubber soles, designed so the climber can stand on small edges, smear on volumes or slabs, and hook with the toes or heel. They fit more tightly than approach or street shoes, but youth shoes should still be comfortable enough for a full class.
items.whyItMatters: Footwork cues (edging, smearing, backstep, quiet feet) only work if the shoe can actually stand on the hold. Shoes that are painfully tight, or so loose they spin, get in the way of learning.
items.howToCoachIt: Let climbers feel the rubber and find the inside edge, outside edge, and toe. Match the drill to the shoe: smear practice on slab, an outside-edge backstep, a careful toe hook on a volume. Watch for numb toes or shoes that slip off the heel.

images.alt: A climbing shoe showing the sticky rubber sole, rand, and edges used for edging, smearing, and hooking.

items.name: Chalk
items.definition: Magnesium carbonate that dries hands; worn in a bag on the waist.
items.kid: Powder that dries your hands.
items.demo: Chalk up properly.

items.name: Carabiner
items.definition: A metal clip with a gate; lockers have a sleeve that closes the gate.
items.kid: A metal clip; lockers screw shut.
items.demo: Lock and unlock.
items.explanation: A carabiner is a metal loop with a spring-loaded gate, used to connect parts of a climbing system. Locking carabiners have a sleeve (screw, twist, or ball-lock) that secures the gate and are the usual choice for attaching a belay device or an auto-belay connector to the belay loop. Non-locking gates are common on quickdraws. Keychain-style clips are not climbing-rated.
items.whyItMatters: An unlocked locker, or a carabiner on a gear loop, is a partner-check failure. Climbers need to know which end of a quickdraw is which, and to confirm that a locker is actually locked.
items.howToCoachIt: Practise opening, closing, and locking a locker out loud (‘locked’) during harness and partner checks. Show a quickdraw’s two carabiners and a locking belay biner side by side. Never use a decorative or keychain clip in a climbing system.

images.alt: A Petzl locking carabiner with a ball-lock sleeve, the kind of locker used on a belay loop.
Several climbing-rated carabiner shapes and gate types, including locking designs, shown together for comparison.
A locking carabiner connecting a tube-style belay device — the usual attachment of a device to the belay loop.

items.name: Belay Device
items.definition: A device that adds friction so the belayer can hold and lower the climber.
items.kid: The tool that helps the belayer hold the rope.
items.demo: Show the brake position.
items.explanation: A belay device is a mechanical tool that adds friction so a belayer can control the rope, take in, pay out, hold a fall, and lower. Tube devices (for example a Black Diamond ATC) are passive and need the belayer to bring the rope into a brake position. Assisted-braking devices (for example a Petzl GRIGRI) help pinch or cam the rope under load, but still need a brake hand and the gym’s taught technique.
items.whyItMatters: The device is only half of the system: it attaches to the belay loop with a locking carabiner, and the brake hand stays on the brake strand. Mixing tube and ABD habits is a common source of errors.
items.howToCoachIt: Show the gym’s tube device and ABD side by side, each on a locker on the belay loop. Practise the brake position on the ground (see Ground School Belay) before any real climber weight, with a backup.

items.name: Quickdraw
items.definition: Two carabiners joined by a sling, used to clip the rope to bolts when leading.
items.kid: Two clips on a strap for lead climbing.
items.demo: See Ground Clipping Practice.
items.explanation: A quickdraw (also a draw or extender) is two carabiners connected by a short, semi-rigid sling (sometimes called a dogbone). One carabiner clips to the bolt or anchor; the other takes the rope. The rope-end carabiner is often a bent gate, and a small elastic keeps that gate oriented — the elastic is not a load-bearing part and belongs on the rope end, not the bolt end.
items.whyItMatters: Draws let the rope run through protection as a leader climbs. How the rope is clipped into the rope-end carabiner is the difference between a correct clip, a back-clip, and a Z-clip.
items.howToCoachIt: On a ground board for Ages 12+ and 14+, name the bolt-end and rope-end carabiners, then practise clipping both hands and reading rope direction. See Ground Clipping Practice, Back-Clip Spotting Board, and Z-Clip Recognition Drill.

images.alt: Several quickdraws, each made of two carabiners joined by a short sling.

items.name: Crash Pad
items.definition: Foam padding below boulders to reduce landing impact.
items.kid: The squishy floor that cushions falls.
items.demo: See Fall Zones Tour.
items.explanation: A crash pad (or bouldering mat) is a thick foam pad used for protection when bouldering. Modern pads are often about 8–15 cm (3–6 in) thick, with two or three layers of foam in a tough cover; some fold for carrying. They help with repeated short landings on hard or uneven ground, and they are also the standard indoor landing surface under bouldering walls.
items.whyItMatters: Pads only help if they cover the actual landing, including the fall zone, with no gaps.
items.howToCoachIt: On the fall-zone tour, have kids point to closed pad coverage and to gaps. Do not stand, stack bags, or film on a pad that is in use.

items.name: Auto Belay
items.definition: A device at the top of a wall that takes in rope and lowers the climber.
items.kid: A machine that belays you.
items.demo: Clip-in check demo.
items.explanation: An auto belay is a mechanical device, usually fixed at the top of a gym lane, that takes in webbing as the climber goes up and lowers them when they sit back. TRUBLUE’s published instructions have climbers clip the carabiner to the belay loop only, test that the webbing retracts, stay in the lane, and unclip only on the ground. In this program, auto-belay use always needs staff permission, and staff clip and unclip for the youngest groups.
items.whyItMatters: Most serious auto-belay incidents involve climbing unclipped or clipped to the wrong point. A consistent clip-in routine, a retraction test, and lane discipline are how the class manages that risk.
items.howToCoachIt: Run Auto-Belay Clip-In Routine and the retraction test before any ascent. Staff-controlled first goes come first. Nobody climbs until a coach confirms the locked clip on the belay loop.

items.name: Rope
items.definition: A stretchy dynamic rope that absorbs fall energy.
items.kid: The stretchy rope that catches you.
items.demo: Pull to feel the stretch.
items.explanation: A climbing rope used for belaying is a dynamic rope, designed to stretch and absorb energy in a fall. It is tied into the harness through both tie-in points, or, in some systems, used with a device; it is not the same as auto-belay webbing.
items.whyItMatters: The stretch is part of how a fall is managed. A rope also needs a dressed tie-in, an adequate tail, and — if the gym requires it — a stopper at the free end so the rope cannot run through the device.
items.howToCoachIt: Let climbers feel a little stretch on a gently weighted top rope (with a backup). Trace the path from tie-in to anchor to device. Contrast a dynamic rope with auto-belay webbing so the two systems are not mixed up.

items.name: Figure-8 Follow-Through
items.definition: The standard tie-in knot; finish with a tail.
items.kid: The knot that ties you to the rope.
items.demo: See Spot the Figure 8.
items.explanation: The figure-eight follow-through (figure-eight loop) is the knot commonly used to tie a climbing rope into a harness. Wikipedia calls it the most common harness tie-in knot: strong, relatively easy to tie and to check, though it can be hard to untie after a heavy load. On a standard sit harness the rope passes through both tie-in points and is retraced; Petzl's figures mark a minimum tail of 10 cm / 3.9 in. Always check the knot before starting to climb.
items.whyItMatters: A knot tied through the belay loop, through only one tie-in point, or with a short un-retraced tail is not the standard gym tie-in taught here.
items.howToCoachIt: Teach the sequence from the Petzl figures: form the eight, pass the tail through both tie-in points, retrace, dress, check the tail. Partners check every time.

items.name: Stopper Knot
items.definition: A knot tied in the rope end so it can't pass through the device.
items.kid: A knot at the rope end.
items.demo: Tie on the end of a practice rope.
items.explanation: A stopper knot (often a barrel knot or double overhand) is tied in the free end of the rope so that end cannot pass through the belay device. Some gyms require it as part of every partner check; follow the gym’s standard.
items.whyItMatters: If the belayer runs out of rope, a stopper is the last thing that can keep the end from pulling through the device. It is only useful if it is actually tied, and it does not replace a dressed figure-8 or a coach check.
items.howToCoachIt: If the gym requires it, add the stopper after the figure-8 is dressed, and include it on the point-and-trace partner check. Practise on a spare rope first.

items.name: Tail
items.definition: The extra rope past a knot.
items.kid: The extra bit of rope left over.
items.demo: Measure a fist-length tail.
items.explanation: The tail is the extra rope past a finished knot. For a figure-8 follow-through, this program uses a fist-length or gym-standard tail after the knot is dressed. Too short a tail can spill; a huge untidy tail is harder to inspect.
items.whyItMatters: A partner check that only glances at the shape of the 8 can miss a short tail. Dressing the knot and measuring the tail belong together.
items.howToCoachIt: In Figure-8 Dressing Lab and Spot the Figure 8, have partners measure a fist-length (or the gym’s stated length) after counting the five strand pairs. Add a stopper only if the gym requires it.

items.name: Flaking
items.definition: Running through a rope into a loose pile so it feeds without tangles.
items.kid: Piling the rope so it doesn't tangle.
items.demo: See Flake and Coil.

items.name: Anchor
items.definition: The fixed point the rope runs through at the top.
items.kid: The strong point at the top.
items.demo: Point to the anchors.

items.name: Top Rope
items.definition: Climbing with the rope already running through an anchor above.
items.kid: Climbing with the rope already at the top.
items.demo: Trace the rope from climber to anchor to belayer.
items.explanation: Top-rope climbing means the rope already runs through a fixed anchor above the climb, and the belayer, usually on the ground, takes in as the climber goes up. If the climber comes off with a snug rope, they hang on a short amount of slack rather than taking a long lead fall.
items.whyItMatters: Top rope is the program’s main roped context before any lead work. Partner checks, commands, take and lower, and belay stance are all learned here, with a backup until the gym’s certification.
items.howToCoachIt: Trace the rope from climber to anchor to belayer. Practise partner check, start-up commands, and take-and-lower on easy routes, with a backup belayer for uncertified belayers. Compare it later with mock lead so climbers feel how the rope path changes.

items.name: Lead Climbing
items.definition: Climbing with the rope from below, clipping quickdraws on the way; falls are longer.
items.kid: Bringing the rope up with you and clipping it as you go.
items.demo: See Mock Lead.
items.explanation: Lead climbing is climbing with the rope coming from below, clipping it into protection (in the gym, usually quickdraws on bolts) as you go. A leader fall is at least twice the distance to the last clipped piece. In this program, mock lead and all lead content are for Ages 12+ and 14+ only.
items.whyItMatters: Leading changes both the climber’s and the belayer’s jobs: clips, slack, stance, and fall length all matter in a way they do not on top rope. Skills are built on the ground and on mock lead with a real backup before any live lead.
items.howToCoachIt: Start with Ground Clipping Practice and Mock Lead (top-rope or auto-belay backup, with staff permission for any auto-belay use). No live leading until the gym’s certification and coach approval.

images.alt: Lead climber clipping a quickdraw on an indoor competition wall. Teaching context for Ages 12+ and 14+ only, usually after mock-lead practice with a backup.

items.name: Back-Clip
items.definition: Clipping a quickdraw so the rope runs from the wall side out toward the climber the wrong way, which can unclip in a fall.
items.kid: Clipping the rope in backward.
items.demo: See What Is Wrong?
items.explanation: A back-clip is a lead-clipping error: the rope is clipped into the quickdraw so that it runs the wrong way — typically not from the wall or bolt side out toward the climber, in the gym’s taught orientation. In a fall, that path can fold the rope over the gate and unclip. This is Ages 12+ and 14+ content.
items.whyItMatters: A back-clip can defeat the protection the climber just placed. Recognizing it on a board is much cheaper than discovering it on a live lead.
items.howToCoachIt: Use Back-Clip Spotting Board on the ground: mark each preset clip correct or back-clipped, explain the rope path, and fix it. Agree the gym’s direction model before debating edge cases. Stay on the ground or on mock lead with a backup.

images.alt: Quickdraws used when teaching rope direction. This photo is the gear, not an example of a back-clip.

items.name: Z-Clip
items.definition: Clipping rope from below the previous draw into the next, creating a Z and heavy drag.
items.kid: Grabbing rope from the wrong spot so it zigzags.
items.demo: Show on a ground clipping board.
items.explanation: A Z-clip happens in lead climbing when the climber takes rope from below the previous quickdraw and clips it into the next one, so the rope forms a Z and creates heavy drag. The correct hand path takes rope from near the harness or knot, above the last clipped draw. This is Ages 12+ and 14+ content.
items.whyItMatters: A Z-clip adds drag that can stall a climber, and it leaves a messy, hazardous rope path that should be fixed before anyone climbs higher, even on mock lead.
items.howToCoachIt: Use Z-Clip Recognition Drill on a two-draw board: demo the correct path, demo the Z, then have climbers practise slowly and identify coach-made mistakes. Cue: grab rope close to the knot.

images.alt: Quickdraws of the kind used on a ground board to demonstrate a correct rope path and a Z-clip. This photo shows the gear, not the error itself.

items.name: Belay
items.definition: Managing the rope to catch and lower a climber.
items.kid: Holding the rope for your climber.
items.demo: See Ground School Belay.
items.explanation: Belaying is managing the rope so a falling climber is caught and, when needed, lowered. The belayer uses a device on the harness belay loop to increase braking force. Devices may be a simple tube (passive) or a cam-assisted device such as a GRIGRI. In a typical setup the climber is tied in with a figure-eight, the rope runs through the top-rope anchor or through protection, and the belayer holds the brake side of the rope. Petzl's REVERSO notice states that the device does not automatically block the rope; the brake strand is always held. Staff permission is required before anyone uses an auto belay; the connector goes to the belay loop only.
items.whyItMatters: Belaying is a partnership skill. The partner check, the commands, and the brake hand are all part of the same system.
items.howToCoachIt: Ground school first, then a top-rope with a backup as your gym requires. Lead belay belongs only in the 12+ and 14+ groups. Load a GRIGRI using the markings on the device (Petzl section 6). Always hold the brake strand.

items.name: Brake Hand
items.definition: The hand that never leaves the brake strand.
items.kid: The hand that never lets go.
items.demo: Shout 'brake hand!' and freeze to check.
items.explanation: The brake hand is the hand that stays on the brake strand — the side of the rope that comes out of the device and is used to add friction. In a tube-device sequence such as PBUS, that hand pulls, goes to the brake position, and slides back up the rope without letting go of the strand.
items.whyItMatters: A break in brake-hand contact is one of the most common belay errors. The device cannot do its job if the brake strand is released.
items.howToCoachIt: Use a freeze cue (‘brake hand!’) during ground school and backed-up wall practice. Watch the slide: the hand must return up the brake strand, not come off it. Petzl’s tube-device notices show the brake side held throughout.

images.credit: Diagram: Petzl — REVERSO technical notice, section 6b: always hold the brake side of the rope

items.name: PBUS
items.definition: A tube-device belay sequence: pull, brake, under, slide.
items.kid: Pull, brake, under, slide.
items.demo: Chant and do it slowly.
items.explanation: PBUS is a tube-device belay sequence: Pull, Brake, Under, Slide. The belayer pulls rope through the device, brings the brake hand to the brake position, brings the other hand under the brake hand, and slides the brake hand back up the rope without leaving the brake strand.
items.whyItMatters: It is a repeatable way to take in rope while keeping brake-hand contact — the habit Ground School Belay is built on. Assisted-braking devices use a related idea but have gym-specific technique that staff must teach separately.
items.howToCoachIt: Chant the four words slowly on a ground-school rope with a backup. Freeze on ‘brake’ to check the brake-hand position, then watch the slide. Do not mix ABD handwork into a PBUS drill in the same turn.

images.alt: Technical hand-sequence diagram of taking in rope in steps, including the brake position and sliding the brake hand back up the strand — a PBUS-style motion, not a cartoon of people.
Petzl tube-device figure showing the brake side of the rope held, the position at the heart of a PBUS cycle.

items.name: Slack
items.definition: Loose rope; also a call for more rope.
items.kid: Loose rope.
items.demo: Show tight and slack.
items.explanation: Slack is extra loose rope in the system. It is also a climber’s call asking the belayer for more rope. Some slack is needed so a leader can clip or move without being short-roped; too much slack makes a fall longer before the rope begins to hold.
items.whyItMatters: Managing slack is the daily job of a belayer: tight enough to manage a fall, loose enough to let the climber move and clip. On an auto belay (staff permission required before anyone uses one), slack from outclimbing the webbing’s retraction is a cue to slow down or stop.
items.howToCoachIt: In Paying Out and Taking In, name both errors — short-roping and too much slack — while a partner walks away and back, with a backup. On top rope, a snug rope at a take should still be the default. If you mention auto-belay slack from a climber outpacing retraction, remind the group that auto-belay use still needs staff permission.

sources.title: How to Use an Auto Belay: Step by Step Instructions

items.name: Take
items.definition: A call to pull rope tight and hold the climber.
items.kid: Say 'take' to have your belayer hold you.
items.demo: Sit back on a tight rope at the first bolt.
items.explanation: ‘Take’ (some gyms say ‘tension’) is the climber’s call asking the belayer to pull the rope tight and hold. The belayer takes in, answers, and holds; the climber sits and confirms weight is on the rope before calling ‘lower’ or climbing on.
items.whyItMatters: A clear take-and-hold is how a climber rests on top rope, comes off a move, or prepares to lower. Mumbled or unmatched words leave the belayer guessing.
items.howToCoachIt: Practise the gym’s exact words in Take and Lower Sequence: call, take tight, sit, confirm, then lower. The brake hand stays on the brake strand the whole time.

images.alt: Petzl diagram of a top-rope belayer in position to take in rope and hold a climber who has called take.
images.credit: Diagram: Petzl — ACCESS BOOK #1, booklet pages 6–7, primary belaying position

items.name: On Belay?
items.definition: Start-up commands: 'On belay?' / 'Belay on.' / 'Climbing.' / 'Climb on.'
items.kid: The question-and-answer before you climb.
items.demo: See Climbing Commands Call-and-Response.
items.explanation: “On belay?” is the American command a climber uses when ready to be belayed. The standard reply is “Belay on.” The usual start-up then continues “Climbing.” / “Climb on.” These commands come after the partner check, not instead of it.
items.whyItMatters: Clear, loud commands are how both people know the belay is on before anyone leaves the ground.
items.howToCoachIt: Practice the call-and-response on the ground, then use it on every top-rope. The belayer is looking up and holding the brake side of the rope (Petzl primary position and REVERSO notice: always hold the brake side; a REVERSO does not automatically block).

images.alt: Petzl Access Book: primary belaying position, belayer looking up and holding the brake side of the rope.
images.credit: Diagram: Petzl — ACCESS BOOK #1, booklet pages 6–7, primary belaying position
images.license: Petzl technical figure; hosted for internal coaching use with credit and source link

items.name: Lower
items.definition: Commands for coming down and ending the belay.
items.kid: Coming down; feet out, sit back.
items.demo: See Astronaut Lowering.
items.explanation: To lower (or lower-off) is for the belayer to take the climber's weight on the device and bring them down. In this program, lower also covers the commands for coming down and ending the belay. The climber typically sits back with feet on the wall; the belayer keeps holding the brake side of the rope. This is different from a downclimb, where the climber climbs down under their own movement.
items.whyItMatters: A clean lower needs a ready belayer, a locked locker, and clear commands. It is how most gym top-ropes finish.
items.howToCoachIt: Practice commands first. The belayer holds the brake strand throughout (Petzl: always hold the brake side; a REVERSO does not automatically block). Contrast a lower with a downclimb lap.

images.alt: Top-rope pair: climber on the wall and belayer below, rope running to a top anchor and back — the system used to lower.
Tube-style belay device in use, brake hand on the brake strand of the rope.

items.name: Falling!
items.definition: Warning calls: 'Falling!' for the belayer, 'Rock!' for anything dropped.
items.kid: Shout it to warn people.
items.demo: Practice shouting loud.
items.explanation: In this vocabulary, ‘Falling!’ is a warning call to the belayer that the climber is coming off. ‘Rock!’ is the warning for anything dropped. They are communication, not a description of landing posture (see landing-position and fear-of-falling).
items.whyItMatters: A loud, early call gives the belayer a moment to brake and look, and it warns people under the wall if something is falling. Quiet or late calls leave partners guessing.
items.howToCoachIt: Practise the gym’s exact words at a real volume, on the ground first, then on a planned top-rope take or a coach-supervised fall practice. Keep ‘Falling!’ and ‘Rock!’ distinct.

items.name: Partner Check
items.definition: Checking each other's harness, knot, device and carabiner before every climb.
items.kid: Checking your buddy's gear before climbing.
items.demo: See Partner Check.
items.explanation: A partner check is each person checking the other's harness, knot, belay device, and locking carabiner before every climb. It includes Petzl's rule to tie in through both tie-in points and always check the knot, and to connect a belay device to the belay loop with a locker that is closed, locked, and loaded on the major axis.
items.whyItMatters: The check is how missed buckles, short tails, and unlocked lockers get caught. It is done every time, including by experienced pairs.
items.howToCoachIt: Use a fixed order (harness, knot, device, locker, commands). Partners point at each item. Coach listens and only prompts if a step is skipped.

images.alt: Sit harness with the parts a partner check names: waist, legs, belay loop, tie-in points.
Finished figure-eight through both tie-in points, tail marked 10 cm / 3.9 inch minimum — a standard knot check.
images.credit: Diagram: Petzl — ACCESS BOOK #1, booklet page 2
images.license: Petzl technical figure; hosted for internal coaching use with credit and source link

items.name: Soft Catch
items.definition: Letting a little rope give during a lead fall so the climber swings in gently.
items.kid: Making a fall feel gentle.
items.demo: Coach-led lead fall demo.
items.explanation: A soft catch (sometimes called a dynamic belay) is a lead-belay catch in which the belayer moves with the fall, or manages a little give in the rope, so the stop is less abrupt than a fully static hard catch. It is a lead skill for Ages 12+ and 14+, and it is not appropriate close to the ground, near ledges, or where a longer fall would swing the climber into a hazard.
items.whyItMatters: On steep ground, a well-timed soft catch can make a higher lead fall more comfortable. Used in the wrong place, the same idea can let a climber hit a ledge or the floor. The concept should be taught before any live practice fall.
items.howToCoachIt: Use Soft-Catch Concept Lab first: define hard and soft catches, discuss when each belongs, and role-play the words used before a planned fall. Live practice comes later, only with certified lead belayers under coach oversight, on steep, clean terrain, at the climber’s pace.

sources.title: A fresh look at fall practice

items.name: Bouldering
items.definition: Climbing short walls without ropes over mats.
items.kid: Climbing low walls with no rope over the mats.
items.demo: Point out the bouldering area.

items.name: Problem
items.definition: A set boulder route.
items.kid: A puzzle route on the boulder.
items.demo: Find a problem's start tag.

items.name: Route
items.definition: A designated path of holds, usually one color.
items.kid: The holds you're allowed to use, all one color.
items.demo: See Climb the Rainbow.
items.explanation: A climbing route is the path a climber follows to the top of a problem, a wall, or a piece of rock. Indoors, holds are usually arranged in marked routes by setters.
items.whyItMatters: Reading a route (which holds, which feet, where to rest) is a skill of its own, practiced in add-on, read-and-point, and observation time.
items.howToCoachIt: Stand on the ground, point hand-foot-hand-foot, then climb the plan. Use easy, well-marked color routes for early practice.

items.name: Start Holds
items.definition: The tagged holds a route starts on.
items.kid: The hold with the tape where you start.
items.demo: Find the start tape.

items.name: Top Out
items.definition: The finish of a problem: matching the last hold or climbing onto the top.
items.kid: The end of the climb.
items.demo: Match the finish hold.
items.explanation: To top out is to finish a climb by going over the top to a standing position. On boulders that often means a mantel: pressing down on the shelf (palms down, like getting out of a pool) until you can stand on it. Momentum notes that mantles can include a palm-down press, a hand-foot match, and leaning in over the feet.
items.whyItMatters: Many indoor problems finish at a last hold, but outdoor boulders and some gym top-outs require this press. It is awkward until it is practiced on a low ledge.
items.howToCoachIt: Start on a low padded ledge or volume. Cue the flip to a palm-down press and a lean over the feet. Agree how they will come down.

images.alt: Climber topping out with a mantle, palms pressing down on the lip to stand onto the shelf.

items.name: Downclimb
items.definition: Climbing back down instead of dropping.
items.kid: Climbing down instead of jumping.
items.demo: See Downclimbing.
items.explanation: To downclimb is to descend by climbing downward, rather than being lowered or rappelling. Momentum's drill stresses eye-to-foot contact: look before you place the foot, and use the legs. On a top-rope, the belayer gives enough slack that the climber is not hanging on the rope.
items.whyItMatters: Downclimbing trains feet, control, and a planned way off a boulder. It also adds easy time on the wall for endurance.
items.howToCoachIt: Climb a vertical or slab route, then climb back down. Coach the belayer's slack. On boulders, agree the downclimb before they leave the ground.

items.name: Fall Zone
items.definition: The area under and around a climber where they might land; keep it clear.
items.kid: The mat space where a climber could fall; stay out.
items.demo: See Fall Zones Tour.
items.explanation: The fall zone is the area under and around a climber where they might land. It should be clear of people, bags, and gaps in the pads. Crash pads are the usual surface in the bouldering fall zone; they work only if they actually cover the landing.
items.whyItMatters: Most avoidable bumps in a youth session happen in a busy fall zone, not on the wall.
items.howToCoachIt: Walk a Fall Zones Tour. One climber (and a spotter, if you are spotting) in a zone at a time. If you include auto belays on the tour, they need staff permission, and the connector clips to the belay loop only.

images.alt: Indoor crash pads covering the landing area under a bouldering wall — the fall zone stays on this surface and stays clear.
Auto belay overview: connector on the belay loop only. Auto-belay use needs staff permission, and the area under the climber still stays clear.
images.credit: Climbing Coach overview diagram, checked against TRUBLUE clip-to-belay-loop guidance
images.license: Climbing Coach overview diagram; hosted with credit and source link

sources.title: How to Use an Auto Belay

items.name: Spotting
items.definition: Guiding a falling boulderer's hips and head toward the mat.
items.kid: Helping a climber land on the mat.
items.demo: See Spotting Practice.
items.explanation: Spotting is standing ready beneath a boulderer (or, in some contexts, a leader close to the ground) to guide a fall toward the mat. The spotter uses soft hands near the hips and guides — they do not try to catch the climber’s full weight.
items.whyItMatters: A well-placed pad still needs a person who can keep the hips and head moving toward that pad. Poor spotting, or spotting a high problem, adds risk instead of reducing it.
items.howToCoachIt: Use Spotting Practice on a low boulder: hands up at the hips, eyes on the climber, mat covering the likely landing, guide rather than catch. Parents may spot the youngest children on very low problems.

images.alt: Spotter behind a low boulder with hands raised near the climber’s hips and pads on the ground, ready to guide a fall toward the mat.

items.name: Landing Position
items.definition: Landing on feet with bent knees, then rolling back, arms in.
items.kid: Bend knees, land, roll back like a turtle.
items.demo: See Learn to Fall.
items.explanation: The program landing is: land on the feet with bent knees, then roll back, arms in. Crash pads are thick foam mats that give a more forgiving surface for the repeated short falls of bouldering; they do not replace a planned landing.
items.whyItMatters: Reaching back with straight arms, or landing on a pad gap, is how wrists and necks get hurt. The landing is a skill to practice on purpose (see Learn to Fall).
items.howToCoachIt: Practice from a sit, then a low hang, on a closed pad with a clear fall zone. Do not start from a height the climber has not landed from lower down.

images.alt: Continuous indoor crash pads under a bouldering wall, the surface a climber should land on.

items.name: Send
items.definition: Completing a route from start to finish without falling.
items.kid: Finishing a climb without falling.
items.demo: Celebrate on the Team Send Board.
items.explanation: In the glossary, to send is to free-climb a route from start to finish, whether as an onsight, flash, or redpoint. In class it means completing the agreed climb without falling or weighting the rope.
items.whyItMatters: The word is useful, but it should not become the only goal; process goals and quality repeats matter more for learning.
items.howToCoachIt: Celebrate a send, then ask what the feet or the partner check looked like. Keep send off process-goal cards.

items.name: Flash
items.definition: Sending on the first try with prior beta.
items.kid: Finishing on your first try.
items.demo: Pick a climb nobody has tried, read it aloud first, then give it one go.

items.name: Onsight
items.definition: Sending on the first try with no beta.
items.kid: First-try send with no hints.
items.demo: Read an onsight route from the ground, then climb it.
items.explanation: An onsight is sending a route or problem on the first attempt, with no prior beta (no advice, no watching a successful go, no rehearsal). A first-try send with beta is a flash; a send after previous falls or practice is a redpoint.
items.whyItMatters: Onsighting is a useful personal challenge and a reason to practise route reading, but it is not a required standard in class. Treating every first try as a high-stakes onsight can make climbers rush or refuse to try.
items.howToCoachIt: Use a quiet preview from the ground, then one honest first try. If you give beta, name it a flash attempt instead. Keep the frame personal — not a contest over who onsighted more.

items.name: Redpoint
items.definition: Sending after practicing the route.
items.kid: Finishing after practicing it.
items.demo: See Redpoint Tactics.

items.name: Project
items.definition: A route worked over multiple sessions.
items.kid: A hard climb you keep practicing.
items.demo: Pick a project and log tries.
items.explanation: A project is a route or boulder you work over more than one session (or many tries in one session) toward a send. The glossary also uses projecting for that longer attempt.
items.whyItMatters: Projects teach planning, one-change-per-try, and patience. They should still leave room in the session for easy movement quality.
items.howToCoachIt: Pick a project that is a stretch, not a desperate fight. Log what changed. Keep process goals alongside the project.

items.name: Beta
items.definition: Information on how to do a route; unrequested beta is 'spray'.
items.kid: The secret plan for a climb.
items.demo: See Beta Swap.

items.name: Crux
items.definition: The hardest move or section.
items.kid: The hardest part.
items.demo: Point to the crux.
items.explanation: The crux is the hardest move or section of a climb. The grade of a route or problem is often defined by the difficulty of that crux.
items.whyItMatters: Finding the crux on the ground changes how a climber rests, paces, and chooses beta. Treating every move as the crux burns energy that was needed later.
items.howToCoachIt: In a route preview, ask the climber to point to the crux and say why it looks hardest, then check that guess after the climb. On a pyramid or project, place the crux work where rest can follow.

items.name: Route Reading
items.definition: Planning a sequence from the ground.
items.kid: Planning your moves before climbing.
items.demo: See Read and Point.
items.explanation: Route reading (also preview or reading) is planning a sequence from the ground: pointing holds, naming rests or awkward sections, and noticing the crux before pulling on.
items.whyItMatters: A short plan reduces surprise mid-route and is the habit behind onsight attempts and calmer top-rope climbs. It also keeps climbers out of other people’s fall lines if they stand aside to look.
items.howToCoachIt: Use Read and Point or Top-Rope Route Preview: from outside the fall line, point holds in order, then partner-check, climb, and name one thing that matched and one that changed. Ages 6–9 can point only the first five holds.

items.name: V-Scale
items.definition: The bouldering difficulty scale, VB/V0 upward.
items.kid: Numbers for how hard a boulder is.
items.demo: See Learn the Grades.

items.name: YDS
items.definition: The North American roped grade scale (5.5, 5.10a…).
items.kid: Numbers for rope climb difficulty.
items.demo: See Guess the Grade.

items.name: Slab
items.definition: Wall less than vertical; balance and footwork terrain.
items.kid: A wall that leans back toward you.
items.demo: See Wall Types.
items.explanation: A slab is a low-angle wall — significantly less than vertical — that emphasizes balance, footwork, and smearing. The wall leans back toward the climber, so hips and feet do more of the work than a hard pull.
items.whyItMatters: Climbers who only pull with their arms often feel worse on slab, not better. Slab is where smearing, precise feet, and a calm shift of weight over a foot (place, shift, move) get learned.
items.howToCoachIt: Start with the wall-angles diagram, then a standing smear or a slow rock-over on a low slab. Cue quiet, precise feet and hips over the feet before the next reach.

images.alt: Climber standing in balance on a low-angle friction slab, weight over the feet, using the sole of the shoe.
Overview diagram of wall angles, with slab shown as less than vertical.
images.credit: Climbing Coach overview diagram, checked against PRG wall-angle wording
images.license: Climbing Coach overview diagram; hosted with credit and source link

items.name: Vertical
items.definition: Wall straight up and down.
items.kid: A straight-up wall.
items.demo: See Wall Types.

items.name: Overhang
items.definition: Wall steeper than vertical; a roof is horizontal.
items.kid: A wall that leans over you.
items.demo: See Wall Types.
items.explanation: An overhang is a wall or rock face angled beyond the vertical. A roof or ceiling is the horizontal end of that spectrum. Steep ground asks for body tension, hips close to the wall, and often techniques such as drop knees, hooks, and careful foot pressure so the feet do not cut.
items.whyItMatters: Movement that works on slab or vertical often fails on an overhang if the hips sag and the feet unload. Teaching wall types first helps climbers choose the right tools. The book reports that climbers who loaded their feet more used up to about 11% less energy and had a lower heart rate.
items.howToCoachIt: Use the wall-angles overview, then let climbers feel the same easy sequence on vertical and on a steep wall. Cue hips in and pressure through the big toes. Save deep drop knees and hard hooks for older groups and easy holds first.

items.name: Arete
items.definition: An outside corner edge of the wall.
items.kid: The corner edge that sticks out.
items.demo: Layback an arete.

items.name: Dihedral
items.definition: An inside corner.
items.kid: An inside corner like an open book.
items.demo: Stem in it.
items.explanation: A dihedral (an open book) is the inside corner formed where two walls meet; it is the opposite of an arete. Dihedrals are the usual place to teach stemming or bridging.
items.whyItMatters: Kids can often rest or climb more easily in a corner than on a flat wall, if they learn to press out instead of only pulling in.
items.howToCoachIt: Walk the gym and find a corner. Name it, then stem it on large holds. Pair the word with the stemming images.

images.alt: Climber in an open-book dihedral, stemming with feet on the two opposing walls.

items.name: Traverse
items.definition: Climbing sideways near the ground.
items.kid: Climbing sideways.
items.demo: See Freeze Traverse.
items.explanation: A traverse is a section of climbing that moves horizontally rather than straight up. A hand traverse, in the glossary, is a traverse without useful footholds.
items.whyItMatters: Traverses let a whole group share one stretch of wall and are ideal for footwork drills (silent feet, hover feet, add-on) because falls are usually short.
items.howToCoachIt: Set a start and finish at the same height, keep the line within a short step of the mat for the youngest groups, and run one climber per fall zone.

items.name: Warm-Up
items.definition: A routine before climbing that goes from light cardio and active joint movement to a little muscle activation, then easy climbing that builds up and matches the day's focus. It lasts about 5 minutes for the youngest groups, about 8 for Ages 6–9 and about 12–18 for Ages 9–12 and older.
items.kid: Getting your body ready.
items.demo: See Pulse Raiser.

items.name: Cool-Down
items.definition: Easy movement and stretching after climbing.
items.kid: Slowing down your body at the end.
items.demo: Not a separate block in these classes; the last game stays low-key, and on the way out climbers say how their forearms feel.

items.name: Pump
items.definition: Forearm fatigue when hard, sustained gripping squeezes off blood flow, so the muscles run short of oxygen and acidity builds.
items.kid: When your arms feel tight and tired.
items.demo: Hold a jug gently, then squeeze hard for the same time; notice which one pumps.
items.explanation: Pump (being pumped) is the accumulation of metabolic waste in the forearms so that even a basic grip becomes very hard to hold.
items.whyItMatters: Pump is the usual limit on easy, longer climbing. Straight arms, relaxed grips, and planned rests delay it; fighting a hard move with bent arms brings it on faster.
items.howToCoachIt: On endurance laps, have the athlete notice early pump, shake out, and rest on a jug or a stem. Choose climbs within ability.

items.name: Endurance
items.definition: The ability to keep climbing a long time; it depends on forearm blood flow, efficient movement and putting weight through the feet.
items.kid: Climbing a long time without getting tired.
items.demo: See Easy Continuous Laps.
items.explanation: Endurance is the ability to keep climbing for longer before the pump takes over. Gresham ties it to efficient movement: graceful, precise climbing conserves energy and lets you climb further on the same effort. Momentum's endurance drills use problems well within ability, not limit projects.
items.whyItMatters: Choosing a hard redpoint to train endurance usually just creates a short, intense fight.
items.howToCoachIt: Easy top-rope laps or linked easy boulders, with one movement cue (straight arms or quiet feet) and planned rests. Downclimbing can add time on the wall if the belayer gives working slack.

items.name: Power Endurance
items.definition: Repeating hard moves without much rest.
items.kid: Doing hard moves again and again.
items.demo: See Power Endurance Circuits.

items.name: Strength
items.definition: The maximum force a climber can produce; it powers single hard moves and also makes every easier move cost less, which helps endurance.
items.kid: How hard you can pull.
items.demo: See Limit Bouldering.
items.explanation: In this program, strength means maximum force for single hard moves, as distinct from endurance (how long you can keep climbing before the pump). The existing demo is limit bouldering.
items.whyItMatters: Kids often call every hard feeling strength. Separating a single hard move from a long easy pump helps you pick the right drill.
items.howToCoachIt: Use easy, quality movement most of the session. When you do a hard move, keep attempts limited and on large holds for younger groups.
