items.name: Threat Perception
items.definition: The brain's prediction that a position or move could cause harm, which makes muscles tense, limits range and adds fear.
items.kid: When your brain thinks a move might hurt, so your body gets stiff.
items.demo: After a scare on a move, rebuild it step by step. See Rebuild the Move.
items.explanation: Consuegra explains that the brain predicts outcomes from past experience. If a move or position is unfamiliar, or once went badly, the brain can tense the muscles and limit range to protect the joint. His example is a climber who hurt a knee on a drop knee and later tenses up before the same move even after the knee has healed. Good experiences and feeling secure loosen that brake; scary or painful ones tighten it.
items.whyItMatters: It explains stiff, hesitant movement after a fall or tweak, and why pushing a scared climber harder backfires.
items.howToCoachIt: Rebuild with easy, successful versions low on the wall, slow breathing, mental rehearsal and the climber's own choice of next step. Praise the calm attempt, not the height.

items.name: Phosphagen System
items.definition: The muscles' quickest energy supply, used in short, hard efforts like each grip on a hold; it refills during brief rests.
items.kid: Your muscles' quick-energy battery that refills when you rest.
items.demo: Do one hard move, rest two minutes, and try again: the quick battery has refilled.
items.explanation: The book explains that each hard grip mostly runs on stored high-energy phosphates. The aerobic system then tops those stores up in the short gaps between holds. The stores refill fast but not instantly: the book reports most of the store back after about two minutes and nearly all of it after about eight. That is why it recommends three to five minutes between maximal efforts.
items.whyItMatters: It gives a clear reason for long rests between hard attempts and short, light gripping between moves.
items.howToCoachIt: For Ages 12+ and 14+, time real rests of three minutes or more between limit tries. Use the battery picture with Ages 9–12.

items.name: Active Recovery
items.definition: Easy climbing or movement between hard efforts to help the forearms recover, instead of sitting still.
items.kid: Climbing very easy stuff between hard climbs to help your arms feel better.
items.demo: Between two hard problems, traverse very easy holds until the arms feel lighter. See Crux-and-Traverse Intervals.
items.explanation: Consuegra reports a study where climbers who traversed easily between attempts had lower blood lactate by the final attempt and got higher on their last try than climbers who walked. He builds interval sessions on this: short hard efforts separated by easy traversing, without ever reaching a total pump.
items.whyItMatters: It turns rests into useful practice and suits youth sessions, which keep everyone moving rather than waiting.
items.howToCoachIt: Use the easiest traverse in the gym, at an effort around 1–2 on a 5-point scale. If the arms get more pumped during the 'rest', it is too hard.

items.name: Forearm Blood Flow
items.definition: How well blood reaches the forearm muscles; light gripping keeps it flowing, hard gripping squeezes it off.
items.kid: Blood bringing fresh energy to your arm muscles. Squeezing too hard blocks it.
items.demo: Hold a jug gently, then squeeze hard, and talk about which one you could hold longer.
items.explanation: The book reports that forearm blood flow is highest at light grip effort, roughly a tenth to a quarter of maximum. It starts dropping as grip gets harder and is choked off at high effort. Long, easy climbing encourages new capillaries within a couple of weeks and new mitochondria over about six. Better climbers re-oxygenate their forearms much faster between holds.
items.whyItMatters: It is the science behind easy endurance laps, light grip and resting before a deep pump.
items.howToCoachIt: For Ages 9–12 and up: easy laps at a mild pump, about 1–2 out of 5, with light grip. For teens: explain why the endurance block is easy on purpose.

items.name: Training Load
items.definition: How much training is done (volume: time, moves, attempts) and how hard it is (intensity: how close to maximum each effort is).
items.kid: How much you climb and how hard it is.
items.demo: Count total moves in a session and rate how hard the hardest ones felt.
items.explanation: The book separates the method (how an exercise is run) from the means (the equipment or terrain). It then splits the load into volume (the total amount of work) and intensity (how much work per unit of time, including nervous-system and mental load). Changing either one changes what a session trains.
items.whyItMatters: Thinking in volume and intensity helps coaches keep youth sessions high in volume and moderate in intensity, and save the true limit efforts for older groups.
items.howToCoachIt: Teens can log both: number of climbs or minutes on the wall, and a 1–5 rating of the hardest efforts. Watch for weeks where both jump at once.

items.name: Training Density
items.definition: How much work time there is compared with rest time, within a session or across a week.
items.kid: How long you climb compared with how long you rest.
items.demo: Climb one minute, rest two, and call that a 1-to-2 density.
items.explanation: The book defines density as the balance of work to recovery, whether that is one minute on and two off in a set or two days of training to one day of rest across a week. Strength and power need low density (long rests); endurance tolerates higher density.
items.whyItMatters: It gives coaches one more dial besides 'harder' or 'more' and explains why limit days have long rests.
items.howToCoachIt: Set density on purpose: long rests for hard boulders, short rests for easy laps. Write the ratio on the whiteboard so teens see it.

items.name: Training Cycle
items.definition: A planned block of training: a macrocycle is the long block toward a goal, made of medium blocks (mesocycles), made of short blocks (microcycles).
items.kid: Planning practice in blocks: a big plan, made of smaller chunks, made of weeks.
items.demo: Show the season on a calendar: the year, the monthly themes, and the weeks inside them.
items.explanation: Consuegra defines the three planning units by length rather than by calendar. A macrocycle is a long block that ends in a higher level of performance. It is split into mesocycles with intermediate goals, which are split into microcycles focused on particular qualities.
items.whyItMatters: This program's monthly themes and weekly plans already work like mesocycles and microcycles; the vocabulary helps older climbers understand why the year is structured.
items.howToCoachIt: With Ages 12+ and 14+, map the current month's theme as a block and the week as a step within it. Keep plans for youth simple and flexible.

items.name: Taper
items.definition: A planned cut in training volume before an important event, keeping intensity, so the climber arrives rested and sharp.
items.kid: Climbing less, but still well, in the days before a big event so you feel fresh.
items.demo: Before an event, keep the same kind of climbing but fewer climbs and longer rests.
items.explanation: The book's tapering guidelines, drawn from sport-science reviews, cut training volume substantially over the final weeks. Sessions are dropped first, then shortened. Intensity is held, not raised, the last sessions aren't used as tests, and recovery is complete. Consuegra stresses that the athlete may not feel great during a taper and that is normal.
items.whyItMatters: It suits Ages 14+ team members before an event, and the 'don't test yourself the day before' idea helps every age.
items.howToCoachIt: For Ages 14+ before a March-style event: fewer, shorter sessions with the same quality, no new hard projects, and no limit testing in the final sessions.

items.name: Multilateral Training
items.definition: Broad, varied practice across many movements, terrains and skills before narrowing to specific goals.
items.kid: Practising lots of different kinds of climbing and moving, not just one thing.
items.demo: Rotate slab, vertical, steep and volumes across a month of the same skill.
items.explanation: In the book's planning models, the general preparation period puts varied, non-specific work ahead of narrow training. It emphasises volume over intensity, introduces different types of movement, corrects basic technique and gathers a wide base of climbing experience. It is the stage where the base for later, more specific work is laid.
items.whyItMatters: This is the base the youth curriculum already rests on: broad movement and technique first, specific strength later.
items.howToCoachIt: Keep sessions varied in terrain and hold type, with technique as the main goal. Save narrow, intense blocks for the older training groups.

items.name: Training Transfer
items.definition: How practice of one thing helps (or gets in the way of) another; the order of skills in a session changes what each one trains.
items.kid: Some practice helps other skills, and the order you do things matters.
items.demo: Do technique while fresh and endurance laps later in the same class.
items.explanation: The book's session-design rules: train technique without fatigue, at the intensity it will really be used. Maximum strength needs full rest between sets. Power needs strength and speed, so it never comes after exhausting work. Endurance work can interfere with strength gains. When strength and power share a session, strength comes first, never the reverse, and endurance sessions are mostly single-focus.
items.whyItMatters: It explains why this program puts the skill block early and the more tiring game or volume later.
items.howToCoachIt: Plan the order: warm-up, technique or hard moves while fresh, then volume or endurance. Don't put dynamic or limit work at the end of a tiring session.

items.name: Climber's Back
items.definition: A rounded upper back and forward shoulders that can develop from lots of pulling without balancing work.
items.kid: When your shoulders round forward from lots of climbing.
items.demo: Stand against a wall and see whether the back of the head and shoulders reach it comfortably. See Wall Angel Hold.
items.explanation: The book describes a typical climbing posture: rounded upper back, an increased lower-back curve, and forward shoulders. Pulling muscles, the chest and the hip flexors tend to become dominant, while the upper-back muscles, deep core and glutes are under-used. It is more pronounced in more advanced climbers. Consuegra recommends relaxing the overactive muscles first, then strengthening the under-used ones.
items.whyItMatters: Teens who climb a lot and also sit at desks are most likely to drift this way, and posture changes can feed shoulder and back pain.
items.howToCoachIt: For Ages 12+ and 14+: upper-back and external-rotation work (Band Face Pulls, Wall Angel Hold, Push-Up Plus), Glute Bridge and Superman Hold, done after climbing. Refer persistent pain to a physio.

items.name: Overuse Injury
items.definition: An injury that builds up from repeated loading without enough recovery, rather than from one fall or knock.
items.kid: An injury that comes from doing too much of the same thing over and over.
items.demo: Ask climbers what 'sore in a normal way' feels like, and how that differs from pain that stays or gets worse.
items.explanation: In the surveys the book reviews, overuse injuries are the most frequent kind in climbing. It rises with climbing grade and is especially common in boulderers. Fingers account for about half of injuries, followed by shoulders, hands and elbows. Prevention comes down to building load gradually, respecting recovery and treating early warning signs seriously.
items.whyItMatters: Keen youth climbers often add sessions quickly; overuse is the most likely injury they will meet.
items.howToCoachIt: Make pain reporting normal. Climbers name where it hurts and when; persistent finger pain or pain that changes how they climb means stop and get it checked.

items.name: Muscle Activation
items.definition: Waking up the muscles a session will use with a few easy reps, without tiring them.
items.kid: Waking up your muscles before you climb, without wearing them out.
items.demo: A few easy squats, push-ups and scapular pulls, then straight to the wall.
items.explanation: In the book's warm-up, activation comes after joint mobilisation, light cardio and range-of-motion work. It starts with big multi-joint movements, then smaller targeted ones, always at a level that activates without fatiguing. The book singles out the hamstrings (before heel hooks) and warns against tiring the rotator cuff, which weakens shoulder control.
items.whyItMatters: It keeps the warm-up short and useful and stops climbers arriving at the wall already tired.
items.howToCoachIt: In the activation part of the warm-up (about 2–4 minutes for Ages 9–12 and older), choose two or three easy movements matched to the day, a few reps each. If anyone is breathing hard or shaking, it was too much.

items.name: Specific Warm-Up
items.definition: The part of the warm-up on the wall, using easy climbing that matches the movement the session will train.
items.kid: Warming up on the wall with easy moves like the ones you'll practise today.
items.demo: On a dynamic day, warm up with gradually bigger reaches on big holds; on a footwork day, quiet-feet laps.
items.explanation: The book splits the warm-up into a general part (getting the body moving and warm) and a specific part on the wall. It argues that the wall part should match the day's focus: a dynamic or big-move day warms up with gradually bigger moves and pulls rather than small crimps and balance moves. It also notes that pulleys are most at risk when crimping without a thorough warm-up.
items.whyItMatters: It makes the short warm-up do double duty: it prepares the body and previews the skill.
items.howToCoachIt: For Ages 9–12, 12+ and 14+, close the warm-up with Ramp-Up Boulders: easy climbs that preview the skill and build up to a good number of easy moves before any small holds. Younger groups use one or two easy climbs at the end of their shorter warm-up.

items.name: Foam Rolling
items.definition: Rolling muscles over a foam roller or ball to ease stiffness and free up movement before training.
items.kid: Rolling your muscles on a foam tube to loosen up.
items.demo: 8–10 slow passes on the calves, then try a high step. See Foam Roll Primer.
items.explanation: Consuegra presents rollers, massage sticks and balls as a way to calm the pain signals that limit range, so a muscle tolerates more stretch. He suggests 8–10 passes on an area as enough. For long-term posture changes he points to a physiotherapist.
items.whyItMatters: It can help a stiff teen get more range for high steps in a short time, without the strength loss of long static stretches.
items.howToCoachIt: Ages 12+ and 14+: a short, optional part of the warm-up on calves, hamstrings, glutes and upper back. Easy pressure, no rolling on joints, the lower back or any injury.

items.name: Contract-Relax Stretching
items.definition: A stretching method that alternates a gentle stretch with a short, steady muscle contraction to gain range; for non-climbing days.
items.kid: Stretch, push gently against it, relax, then stretch a bit more.
items.demo: On a non-climbing day, try it on the hamstrings. See Contract-Relax Hamstring Stretch.
items.explanation: The book offers contract-relax stretching as part of separate mobility work aimed at posture and long-term range, apart from the warm-up. It reports that the method gains more range than passive stretching. In the basic version the muscle is stretched lightly, tensed against resistance for about 10–15 seconds, relaxed, and then stretched for another 15–20 seconds. A variation adds a contraction of the opposite muscle. Two to four rounds per muscle is the range it gives.
items.whyItMatters: It gives teens an off-day tool for stiff hamstrings or hips without stretching before climbing, which the book shows lowers strength for a while.
items.howToCoachIt: Teach it to Ages 12+ and 14+ as home mobility, never in the warm-up. Gentle effort, no pain, no bouncing.

items.name: Three-Pad Edge
items.definition: A deep fingerboard edge or hold, about 24 mm, wide enough for the first three finger pads; the only fingerboard edge used before about 16.
items.kid: The biggest edge on a finger board, deep enough for three finger pads.
items.demo: Lay a hand on the 24 mm edge and count the finger pads that fit. See Three-Pad Edge Hang.
items.explanation: The book's under-16 options for finger strength are bar hangs and hangs on a 24 mm edge or three-pad hold, which it calls a good hold. Smaller edges and max-weight protocols are kept for climbers over 16 with two or more years of systematic training. On a three-pad edge an open hand or half crimp is possible, never a full crimp.
items.whyItMatters: It gives coaches and teens one clear line: if it isn't the three-pad edge, it isn't for under-16s.
items.howToCoachIt: Ages 12+ and 14+ only, after bar hangs and after a full warm-up. Short hangs with seconds in reserve, long rests, and a log of total hang time.
